For \(k=2\), take
\[
N_1=13579,\qquad N_2=24681.
\]
Suppose a non-decreasing five-digit number \(x=x_1x_2x_3x_4x_5\) matches neither \(N_1\) nor \(N_2\) in any position. Then:
\[
x_1\notin\{1,2\}\Rightarrow x_1\ge 3.
\]
Since \(x_2\ge x_1\) and \(x_2\notin\{3,4\}\), we get \(x_2\ge 5\).  
Then \(x_3\ge x_2\ge 5\) and \(x_3\notin\{5,6\}\), so \(x_3\ge 7\).  
Then \(x_4\ge x_3\ge 7\) and \(x_4\notin\{7,8\}\), so \(x_4\ge 9\).  
Finally \(x_5\ge 9\), but \(x_5\notin\{1,9\}\), impossible because the only digit \(\ge 9\) is \(9\).

Thus every non-decreasing five-digit number matches \(13579\) or \(24681\) in at least one position.

For \(k=1\), any single five-digit number forbids at most \(5\) digits, so choose a digit \(c\in\{1,\dots,9\}\) not among its digits. Then \(ccccc\) is non-decreasing and matches no position. Hence \(k=1\) is impossible.

\[
\boxed{2}
\]
